questions.stem: What are the four types of tissue in the body?
questions.why: Epithelial, connective, muscle, and neural (nervous) tissue. Adipose and glandular tissue are subtypes within these categories, not categories of their own.

options.why: Epithelial tissue is missing from this list.
Adipose is a subtype of connective tissue.
Connective tissue is missing from this list.

questions.stem: Epithelial tissue is avascular. What does that mean for how it receives its blood supply?
questions.why: One side of epithelium is unattached and the other is connected to the body via connective tissue — and that connective tissue is where the blood supply comes from, since epithelium is avascular.

options.why: Avascular means no vessels run within it.

options.t: From fluid bathing its free surface
options.why: Nutrients reach it from the attached side, not the free one.

options.t: It requires no blood supply at all
options.why: All living tissue needs a blood supply.

options.t: From the connective tissue beneath it

questions.stem: Which property of epithelial tissue makes it well suited to covering exposed surfaces?
questions.why: Epithelium can regenerate quickly after injury, which suits tissue that covers the intestinal lining, the outer surface of the skin, and the inner lining of the mouth.

options.t: It secretes a protective layer of adipose tissue
options.why: Adipose is connective tissue, not an epithelial secretion.

options.t: It can regenerate itself quickly if injured
It contracts and relaxes to accommodate movement
options.why: Contraction is a muscle tissue property.

options.t: It is richly supplied with its own blood vessels
options.why: Epithelium is avascular by definition.

questions.stem: Which are the four functions of epithelial tissue?
questions.why: Physical protection, permeability, sensation, and specialized secretions. Any substance entering or leaving the body must cross an epithelium.

options.why: Contraction and blood cell production belong to other tissues.
Storage is a connective tissue role.
Insulation and conduction belong to other tissues.

questions.stem: Gland cells produce secretions onto the surface of epithelium or into the interstitial fluid and blood. Which of the following are among those secretions?
questions.why: Specialized secretions from gland cells run from hormones to sweat to saliva to mucus.

options.why: Those are connective tissue fibers.
Those are blood components.
Those are produced by organs, not gland cells of epithelium.

questions.stem: Which statement about connective tissue is correct?
questions.why: Connective tissue is the most abundant and widely dispersed tissue in the body. It binds structures, supports and protects, fills spaces, stores fat, produces blood cells, and repairs damaged tissue.

options.t: It is confined to the musculoskeletal system
options.why: It is found throughout the entire body.

options.t: It is found only where two bones meet
options.why: That describes cartilage at a joint only.

options.t: It is the least vascular of the four types
options.why: Connective tissue includes blood, the most vascular tissue.

options.t: It is the most abundant and widely dispersed

questions.stem: What are the three basic components of connective tissue?
questions.why: Specialized cells, extracellular protein fibers, and ground substance — the amorphous gelatinous substance sitting between the fibers and cells.

options.why: Vessels and nerves run through it but are not components.
Those are both specialized cells, only one component.
Those are all types of fiber, only one component.

questions.stem: Which connective tissue cell secretes heparin and histamine?
questions.why: Mast cells secrete heparin, which prevents blood clotting, and histamine, for the inflammatory and allergic response.

options.why: Those store body fat.
Those produce the fibers.
Those engulf and devour microorganisms.

questions.stem: Which connective tissue cell engulfs and devours unwanted microorganisms?
questions.why: Macrophages engulf and devour unwanted microorganisms. Fibroblasts produce fibers, adipocytes store fat, and melanocytes produce melanin.

options.why: Those produce connective tissue fibers.
Those produce melanin.
Those secrete heparin and histamine.

questions.stem: Melanocytes produce melanin, which does what?
questions.why: Melanocytes produce melanin, which gives skin its color. They are found in the epidermis.

options.why: That is histamine's role.

options.t: Prevents water loss through the skin
options.why: That is keratin's role.
That is the adipocyte's role.

questions.stem: Which type of connective tissue fiber makes up ligaments and tendons?
questions.why: Collagenous fibers form ligaments and tendons. Elastic fibers allow stretching, as in the vocal cords, and reticular fibers form delicate supporting networks in the spleen.

options.why: Those allow stretching, as in the vocal cords.
Muscle fibers are not connective tissue fibers.
Those form delicate supporting networks.

questions.stem: Blood and lymph fluid belong to which classification of connective tissue?
questions.why: Fluid connective tissue is blood and lymph. Unlike the other classes it does not connect structures or provide mechanical support.

options.why: Dense tissue is a subtype of connective tissue proper.
That includes cartilage and bone.
That gives skin its resistance to compression.

questions.stem: Cartilage and bone belong to which classification of connective tissue?
questions.why: Supporting connective tissue has more dense fibers, protects soft tissue, and takes on the weight of the body. It includes cartilage and bones.

options.why: Loose tissue fills spaces rather than supporting weight.
That is blood and lymph.
Dense tissue does not bear the body's weight.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of skeletal muscle tissue has the most direct bearing on bleeding from an injury?
questions.why: Skeletal muscle is rich in blood supply, so injuries to it bleed heavily. It is also voluntary, striated, and connected to the skeleton by tendons.

options.t: It attaches via tendons, which limits vessel involvement
options.why: Tendon attachment does not limit vessel involvement.

options.t: It is striated, which causes tissue to tear along fiber lines
options.why: Striations affect appearance, not bleeding.

options.t: It is voluntary, which allows the patient to control the injury
options.why: Voluntary control does not stop hemorrhage.

options.t: It is rich in blood supply, which causes heavy bleeding

questions.stem: Where is smooth muscle tissue found and what are its characteristics?
questions.why: Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary, made of elongated spindle-shaped cells in hollow organ walls — intestines, stomach, blood vessels, uterus.

options.t: Striated, involuntary, found in the heart
options.why: That describes cardiac muscle.

options.t: Striated, voluntary, attached to the skeleton
options.why: That describes skeletal muscle.
Smooth muscle is involuntary.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a function of smooth muscle tissue?
questions.why: Smooth muscle constricts blood vessels, breaks down and digests food, moves fluid through the body, and eliminates waste. Posture and expression are skeletal muscle roles.

options.why: That is a cardiac muscle function.
That is a skeletal muscle function.
That is a skeletal muscle function.

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle tissue relies on what to stimulate contraction, and what unique structure binds its cells?
questions.why: Cardiac muscle, also called myocardium, is involuntary and relies on pacemaker cells. Its cells are tightly connected through intercalated disks, a structure unique to cardiac tissue.

options.why: Cardiac muscle has no tendons.
Cardiac muscle is involuntary and uses intercalated disks.
Striations are structural, not a binding mechanism.

questions.stem: What are the two basic cell types of nervous tissue and their roles?
questions.why: Neurons are the basic structure of neural tissue and act as conduits sending signals to and from other neurons, muscles, and glands. Neuroglia are supporting cells providing nourishment, protection, and insulation.

options.why: Both are parts of a neuron, not cell types.
Astrocytes are supporting cells, not conductors.
The two roles are reversed here.

questions.stem: Serous membranes line which body cavities?
questions.why: Serous membranes line cavities with no opening to the outside — thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic. Mucous membranes are the ones lining cavities exposed to the outside.

options.why: That is the cutaneous membrane.
Those are lined by synovial membranes.
Those are lined by mucous membranes.

questions.stem: What is the difference between parietal and visceral pleura?
questions.why: Parietal adheres to the cavity wall, visceral adheres to the outside of the organ, and serous fluid between them maintains lubrication.

options.t: Parietal lines the wall; visceral covers the organ
Parietal secretes fluid; visceral absorbs it
options.why: Both layers contribute to the serous fluid.

options.t: Parietal is abdominal; visceral is thoracic
options.why: Both types appear in both cavities.

options.t: Parietal covers the organ; visceral lines the wall
options.why: The two layers are reversed here.

questions.stem: Which membrane type contains goblet cells that produce mucus?
questions.why: Mucous membranes line the cavities exposed to the outside — nose, mouth, respiratory, urinary, reproductive, and digestive tracts — and contain goblet cells that produce mucus.

options.why: Those line joint cavities.
Those line closed cavities and secrete serous fluid.
That is the skin.

questions.stem: Synovial membranes are made up entirely of what, and what do they surround?
questions.why: Synovial membranes are made entirely of connective tissue and form an incomplete lining within the cavities of the synovial joints, surrounding the synovial fluid.

options.why: Adipose is not the synovial membrane's composition.

options.t: Epithelium; the serous fluid of the thorax
options.why: Serous membranes contain epithelium; synovial do not.

options.t: Epithelium and connective tissue; the outer surface of bones
options.why: Synovial membranes are connective tissue only.

options.t: Connective tissue; the synovial fluid within joint cavities

questions.stem: The integumentary system consists of the skin plus which accessory structures?
questions.why: The integumentary system is the largest system in the body and the interface between the body and the outside world. It consists of skin plus hair, nails, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands.

options.t: Sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and the fascia
options.why: Hair and nails are missing from this list.

options.t: Hair, nails, lymph nodes, and blood vessels
options.why: Lymph nodes belong to the lymphatic system.

options.t: Hair, nails, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands
Nails, hair follicles, and the subcutaneous muscle layer
options.why: The muscle layer is not part of the integument.

questions.stem: How does the integumentary system perform temperature regulation?
questions.why: Temperature regulation works through constriction and dilation of blood vessels — shunting blood toward or away from the surface.

options.why: Melanin affects pigmentation, not heat.

options.t: Hair follicles trap or release insulating air
options.why: Hair contributes but vessel calibre is the mechanism.
Oil production affects skin condition, not temperature.

questions.stem: Which integumentary function involves fluid shifting to injury sites to fight infections and injuries?
questions.why: The inflammatory response shifts fluid to injury sites. Fluid regulation is the separate function of preventing excessive fluid loss from the body.

options.why: That works through vessel constriction and dilation.
That detects touch, pressure, and temperature.
That prevents excessive fluid loss.

questions.stem: Which layer of skin is the outermost, and what are its characteristics?
questions.why: The epidermis is the outermost layer: waterproof, tough, and containing the melanocytes that produce melanin.

options.why: That is the middle layer.
That is the skin as a whole.
That is the innermost layer.

questions.stem: Which layer of the skin is the thickest, and which specialized structures does it contain?
questions.why: The dermis is the middle and thickest layer, tough and elastic, holding nerve endings, blood vessels, sweat glands, hair follicles, and sebaceous (oil) glands.

options.why: That is the outermost and thinner layer.
That is the innermost layer.
That is not a skin layer.

questions.stem: The subcutaneous tissue lies between which two structures, and what is it composed of?
questions.why: The subcutaneous layer is the innermost layer of skin, sitting beneath the dermis and above the muscle, composed of adipose tissue. It insulates, protects, and stores energy as fat.

options.t: Beneath the muscle and above the bone; composed of fascia
options.why: It lies above muscle, not below it.

options.t: Beneath the epidermis and above the dermis; composed of connective tissue
options.why: The dermis lies directly beneath the epidermis.

options.t: Above the epidermis; composed of keratin
options.why: Nothing lies above the epidermis.

options.t: Beneath the dermis and above the muscle; composed of adipose tissue

questions.stem: Sebaceous glands produce sebum. What does sebum do?
questions.why: Sebum prevents excessive drying of skin and hair, prevents water loss, and keeps skin pliable. Sweat glands are the ones releasing excess heat.

options.why: Sebum lubricates rather than fights infection.
That is the sweat glands' role.
That is melanin's role.

questions.stem: How many bones are in the body?
questions.why: There are 206 bones in the body. Their functions are support, leverage, protection, storage, calcium maintenance, and blood cell production.

options.why: That overcounts the skeleton.
That undercounts the skeleton.
That undercounts the skeleton.

questions.stem: Which structure produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, and what is that process called?
questions.why: Red marrow makes RBCs, WBCs, and platelets, in a process called hematopoiesis.

options.why: The growth plate lengthens bone.
Yellow marrow stores fat rather than making cells.
Compact bone is structural, not hematopoietic.

questions.stem: Which two substances does the skeletal system store?
questions.why: The skeleton stores marrow and calcium, and it maintains calcium levels by releasing and storing it as the body requires.

options.why: Iron is stored in the liver and spleen.
Neither is the pair named for skeletal storage.
Glycogen is stored in liver and muscle.

questions.stem: Which group are all classified as long bones?
questions.why: Long bones are longer than they are wide, found in the limbs, with a shaft and two ends permitting movement at joints. The humerus, ulna, radius, femur, tibia, and fibula are the examples.

options.why: Those are irregular bones.
Those are flat bones.
Those are short bones.

questions.stem: Short bones are described how, and where are they found?
questions.why: Short bones are as wide as they are long, found in the wrists and feet, and assist in fine movement. They are compact and strong — phalanges, metacarpals, and metatarsals.

options.t: Longer than wide, found in the limbs
options.why: That describes long bones.

options.t: As wide as long, in the wrists and feet
Thin and broad, encasing vital organs
options.why: That describes flat bones.

options.t: Uniquely shaped for a specific function
options.why: That describes irregular bones.

questions.stem: The sternum, ribs, scapulae, and skull are classified as which type of bone?
questions.why: Flat bones are thin and broad, usually encasing vital organs and curving to do so.

options.why: Those have unique shapes for specific functions.
Those are longer than they are wide.
Those are as wide as they are long.

questions.stem: The mandible, facial bones, vertebrae, and pelvis are classified as which type of bone?
questions.why: Irregular bones have unique shapes and functions, designed to perform a specific function.

options.why: Those are found in the limbs.
Those are in the wrists and feet.
Those are thin and broad, encasing organs.

questions.stem: What are the two layers all bones are composed of?
questions.why: Compact (solid or cortical) bone is mostly solid with a central marrow canal. Spongy (cancellous or trabecular) bone is a lacy network of bony rods.

options.why: Those are marrow types, not bone layers.
Periosteum is a covering, not a bone layer.
Those are regions of a long bone, not layers.

questions.stem: How is spongy bone structured, and why?
questions.why: Spongy bone is a lacy network of bony rods oriented along lines of stress — the orientation is what increases weight-bearing capacity.

options.why: Concentric rings describe compact bone structure.
Spongy bone is bony rods, not cartilage.

options.t: A lacy network oriented along stress lines
A solid mass with a hollow central canal
options.why: That describes compact bone.

questions.stem: The diaphysis of a long bone is which region, and what does it contain?
questions.why: The diaphysis is the shaft, composed of compact bone tissue. It is a hollow tube — which lightens the bone — with a medullary or marrow canal holding blood vessels and yellow marrow.

options.t: The zone holding the growth plate
options.why: That is the metaphysis.
That is the epiphysis.

options.t: The fibrous covering of the bone
options.why: That is the periosteum.

questions.stem: The epiphysis is located where, and what does it contain?
questions.why: The epiphysis sits at the end of each diaphysis, is made of spongy bone, contains red marrow, and lightens the bone.

options.t: Between the shaft and the end, containing cartilage
options.why: That is the metaphysis.

options.t: At the end of each diaphysis, made of spongy bone and containing red marrow
At the center of the shaft, made of compact bone and containing yellow marrow
options.why: That is the diaphysis.

options.t: Surrounding the entire bone as a fibrous membrane
options.why: That is the periosteum.

questions.stem: What is found in the metaphysis during childhood and adolescence, and what happens to it in adulthood?
questions.why: The metaphysis sits between the diaphysis and epiphysis and holds the epiphyseal plate — cartilage replaced by bone as the bone lengthens. It closes at adulthood, making a mature adult bone.

options.t: The growth plate, which closes at adulthood
The marrow canal, which fills with bone
options.why: The marrow canal stays open in the shaft.

options.t: Periosteum, which is shed after growth
options.why: Periosteum persists throughout life.

options.t: Red marrow, which turns yellow at adulthood
options.why: Marrow conversion is separate from the growth plate.

questions.stem: When does bone formation begin, and by what process do bones develop from tissue and cartilage?
questions.why: Bone formation begins at 6 weeks in utero post fertilization. Bones start as tissue and cartilage and become bone through ossification — replacing tissue with bone by depositing calcium salts. Osteogenesis is the actual formation of the bones.

options.t: At 6 weeks in utero, through ossification
At birth, through the process of osteogenesis
options.why: Bone formation is well underway before birth.

options.t: In the first year, by calcifying the marrow
options.why: Formation starts in utero, not after birth.

options.t: At 12 weeks in utero, through hematopoiesis
options.why: Hematopoiesis is blood cell formation.

questions.stem: What are fontanelles and what is their purpose?
questions.why: Fontanelles are the soft spots — sheets of tough connective tissue between the flat bones of the infant skull. They soften and expand during childbirth and are gradually replaced as the skull bones fuse.

options.t: Tissue sheets letting the skull flex
Spongy areas that store red marrow
options.why: Fontanelles are connective tissue, not bone.
Those are epiphyseal plates.
Fontanelles are tissue, not openings for vessels.

questions.stem: What is proprioception?
questions.why: Proprioception is awareness of motion and position of a body part — a function associated with joints, which are formed wherever two bones come into contact.

options.t: The ability of a joint to bear weight
options.why: Weight-bearing is a structural property, not a sense.

options.t: The secretion of synovial fluid into a joint cavity
options.why: That is the synovial membrane's function.

options.t: Awareness of the motion and position of a body part
The connection of two bones by fibrous tissue
options.why: That describes a fibrous joint.

questions.stem: How are most joints named?
questions.why: Most joints are named after the two bones they connect — the sternoclavicular joint connects the sternum and the clavicle.

options.why: Movement type gives the physiological name, not the joint name.

options.t: After the two bones they connect
After the tissue that forms them
options.why: Tissue gives the anatomical classification.

options.t: After the muscle acting across them
options.why: Muscles are named separately from joints.

questions.stem: A fibrous joint permits what degree of movement, and what is its physiological name?
questions.why: Fibrous joints are synarthroses, permitting no movement. Examples are teeth in the mandible, the tibia and fibula connection, and the skull bones.

options.why: That is a synovial joint.
That is a cartilaginous joint.
That is not one of the three classifications.

questions.stem: Intervertebral disks and the connection between ribs and costal cartilage are examples of which joint type?
questions.why: Cartilaginous joints are amphiarthroses, connected via cartilage and allowing little movement. Ribs with costal cartilage and intervertebral disks are the examples.

options.why: Synovial joints permit free movement.
Serous is not a joint classification.
Fibrous joints permit no movement at all.

questions.stem: The wrist, elbow, shoulder, hip, and ankle are all which type of joint?
questions.why: Synovial joints are diarthroses, allowing free movement. They are complex joints within a joint cavity containing synovial fluid.

options.why: Those permit only slight movement.
Those permit no movement.
That is not one of the three classifications.

questions.stem: Match each specialized connective tissue cell to what it does.
questions.why: Five cells, five jobs. Mast cells are the ones to know cold for allergy and anaphylaxis — histamine release is what drives that presentation.
pairs: Produce melanin, which gives skin its color

questions.stem: Match each joint type to the movement it allows.
questions.why: Anatomical name comes from the tissue in the joint; physiological name comes from the movement allowed. Syn is none, amphi is a little, di is free.
pairs: No movement — skull bones, teeth in the mandible
Little movement — intervertebral disks, costal cartilage
Free movement — wrist, elbow, shoulder, hip, ankle

questions.stem: Match each region of a long bone to its description.
questions.why: Shaft, end, and the growth zone between them. Red marrow is in the epiphysis and makes blood cells; yellow marrow is in the diaphysis.
pairs: The shaft — compact bone with a medullary canal and yellow marrow
The end of the bone — spongy bone containing red marrow
Between shaft and end — site of the epiphyseal growth plate
